data.title: Harmony in Diversity: Multi-domain Contrastive Policy Optimization for Large Reasoning Models
data.author: Zongji Yu, Wenshui Luo, Yiliu Sun, Hao Fang, Hanrui Xu, Runmin Cong, Chaochao Lu, Chen Gong
data.summary: Multi-domain capabilities are critical for practically applicable Large Reasoning Models (LRMs). Therefore, mixed-domain Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a crucial process to jointly train a single LRM with mixed domain data, but it often induces capability trade-offs among different domains. Existing methods attribute this issue to competing cross-domain interactions, and mitigate them by isolating learning directions and balancing learning progress. However, our observation suggests that they also impede supportive knowledge sharing across domains, which make it difficult to match or surpass single-domain performance. To address this problem, we propose \textbf{M}ulti-domain \textbf{C}ontrastive \textbf{P}olicy \textbf{O}ptimization (MCPO), which applies contrastive learning to achieve diverse knowledge sharing and competition. We first localize the interaction units on critical reasoning segments, and then formulate mutually augmented examples to capture both positive and negative interactions. Subsequently, we design complementary contrastive objectives for cross-domain knowledge sharing and intra-domain knowledge consolidation. Overall, we utilize diverse cross-domain interactions to achieve compatibility across domains and discriminability within each domain to form a harmonious reasoning space. Experimental results across a broad range of domains show that MCPO significantly outperforms existing methods mitigating interactions over 3.17 average points, and even surpasses single-domain training over 1.05 average points.

oai:arXiv.org:2605.25443v3.label: Harmony in Diversity: Multi-domain Contrastive Policy Optimization for Large Reasoning Models

data.title: JuICE: A Benchmark for Evaluating LLM-Judge in Identifying Cultural Errors
data.author: Jiho Jin, Junho Myung, Juhyun Oh, Junyeong Park, Rifki Afina Putri, Sunipa Dev, Vinodkumar Prabhakaran, Alice Oh
data.summary: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed to users around the world, they are integrated into everyday tasks across diverse cultural contexts, from drafting personal communications to brainstorming creative ideas. These tasks are inherently cultural: they require contextual appropriateness, symbolic resonance, and tacit cultural expectations that native speakers draw on instinctively, meaning that a response can be factually plausible yet unmistakably wrong to a local reader. Existing cultural benchmarks have treated culture as a flat set of facts via fact verification or norm entailment methods, and have adopted LLM-as-a-Judge without examining whether they can capture such thick cultural errors. To address this gap, we present JuICE (Benchmark for LLM-Judge in Identifying Cultural Errors), a multilingual dataset of 7,470 span-level annotations of cultural and linguistic errors in long-form LLM responses. It covers 1,050 query-response pairs from four countries (the United States, South Korea, Indonesia, and Bangladesh), in both English and their countries' main languages. Using JuICE, we find that even the strongest LLM-judge achieves only an F1 of 0.51 in the erroneous span detection task. Furthermore, LLM-judges consistently miss thick cultural errors that local residents readily identify. Our findings suggest that robust cultural evaluation must move beyond surface-level detection toward frameworks that account for the depth and situatedness of cultural meaning.

data.title: K-BrowseComp: A Web Browsing Agent Benchmark Grounded in Korean Contexts
data.author: Nahyun Lee, Dongkeun Yoon, Guijin Son, Geewook Kim, Dayoon Ko, Jeonghun Park, Haneul Yoo, Jaewon Cho, Junghun Park, Changyoon Lee, Kyochul Jang, Jaeyeon Kim, Eunsu Kim, Woojin Cho, Seungone Kim
data.summary: Frontier model evaluations are shifting from foundational capabilities (e.g., instruction following and reasoning) toward compositional, agentic ones, but Korean agentic benchmarks remain scarce. We introduce K-BrowseComp, a web-browsing agent benchmark grounded in Korean contexts, consisting of 400 problems. The 300-problem K-BrowseComp-Verified subset is manually constructed and validated by native Korean speakers. On this subset, frontier LLMs, including GPT-5.5, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, and GLM-5.1, reach only 30.00--45.67\%, a substantial drop from BrowseComp, while Korean LLMs released through Korea's Proprietary AI Foundation Model program obtain only 0.00--10.33\%. We further construct a 100-problem synthetic split using hard few-shot exemplars and failure-mode-targeted generation to exploit the asymmetry between solving and creating web browsing problems. On the adversarially filtered synthetic diagnostic split, the strongest model reaches only 26.00\%, and we report this split separately as a targeted stress test. We publicly release our data and code.

data.title: RubricReviewer: From Direct Critique to Rubric-Driven Review via Agentic Evidence Synthesis and Human-Aligned Generation
data.author: Shuyu Guo, Wenxiang Hu, Yuyue Zhao, Lun Zhou, Yougang Lyu, Xiaohui Yan, Zhaochun Ren
data.summary: Peer review at major venues is under unprecedented submission pressure, motivating the use of large language models (LLMs) as review assistants. Existing LLM-based reviewers, however, face two structural limitations. First, they map manuscripts directly to reviews, leaving the underlying rubric implicit and entangling its derivation with the judgement. Second, the prevailing paradigms each capture only half of a good review: training-free agents gather broad evidence but produce undirected critiques, while training-based reviewers inherit human discriminative judgement together with its noise and uneven coverage. We introduce RubricReviewer, a fully rubric-driven framework that addresses both limitations. It makes rubric generation an explicit intermediate step, so that both review generation and the final assessment are conditioned on paper-adaptive rubrics. It further combines a training-free agent (Scout) that gathers external evidence with a human-aligned trained model (Aligner) that consumes this evidence, fusing the strengths of both supervision sources. Experiments on real-world submissions show that RubricReviewer produces reviews that are markedly more comprehensive and more discriminative than prior systems, and exhibits the strongest robustness against adversarial prompt-injection attacks. Ablation studies further confirm the necessity of each component.

oai:arXiv.org:2608.00005v2.label: RubricReviewer: From Direct Critique to Rubric-Driven Review via Agentic Evidence Synthesis and Human-Aligned Generation

data.title: Prompt Privilege in Large Language Models: Measuring and Mitigating Barriers to Equitable AI Access
data.author: Lier Jin, Lan Hu, Binqi Shen, Hanyu Cai, Yuting Xin
data.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in healthcare, education, public services, and everyday decision making. They should provide comparable assistance regardless of users' literacy, communication style, or prompt-engineering expertise. However, research on prompt robustness primarily focuses on adversarial attacks, prompt injection, and prompt optimization, overlooking whether semantically equivalent requests receive different responses simply because they are phrased differently. We call this accessibility challenge "Prompt Privilege": users with greater prompting expertise obtain better model performance despite expressing the same underlying intent. To address this problem, we propose the Prompt Equity Score (PES), a metric for evaluating performance consistency across user populations, and the Prompt Equity Transformer (PET), an LLM-based agent that automatically transforms user requests into semantically equivalent prompts while preserving their intent. PET shifts prompt optimization from users to AI systems, serving as an accessibility layer between users and foundation models. Experiments on MedQA reveal measurable prompt privilege, with statistically significant performance disparities between low-literacy and expert-prompting cohorts. Applying PET reduces these differences, with no pairwise cohort differences reaching statistical significance in our evaluation. These results suggest that accessibility-oriented prompt normalization can improve equitable AI access. By introducing prompt privilege as a new dimension of AI accessibility and PET as a practical solution, this work advances system-centered accessibility and provides a foundation for fairer, more trustworthy, and more inclusive AI systems.

oai:arXiv.org:2608.08942v2.label: Prompt Privilege in Large Language Models: Measuring and Mitigating Barriers to Equitable AI Access

data.title: Rollback the World, Keep the Reflection: Rollback-Induced Reflection for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
data.author: Yi Yu, Liuyi Yao, Yaliang Li, Enshu Wang, Libing Wu
data.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly tackle long-horizon tasks through multi-step environment interaction, yet a single erroneous action can alter subsequent states and observations, causing errors to compound over time. Existing methods either correct the context without repairing altered environment states or restore earlier states while discarding useful experience, making it difficult to both eliminate failure conditions and avoid repeating past mistakes. We argue that reliable recovery should instead be treated as a rollback-boundary control problem that jointly determines when to intervene, where to resume, and what information should survive recovery. Based on this view, we propose Rollback-Induced Reflection (RIR), a unified recovery framework that restores execution to a selected prior state while carrying forward reusable knowledge distilled from the abandoned trajectory to guide subsequent decisions. We further characterize recovery through a unified operator over rollback depth and retained memory, providing a general view of state restoration and knowledge retention. Experiments on three long-horizon benchmarks show that RIR consistently improves average task performance across multiple LLM backbones, with structured reflection memory preserving useful experience and selective rollback enabling efficient recovery.

oai:arXiv.org:2609.18304v4.label: Rollback the World, Keep the Reflection: Rollback-Induced Reflection for Long-Horizon LLM Agents

data.title: Wolof-Adapted Industry-Ready Open-Weight Language Models
data.author: Gw\'enol\'e Lecorv\'e, Delphine Charlet, Pierre Adam, Floriane Behanzin, Lionel Delphin-Poulat, Johannes Heinecke, G\'eraldine Damnati, Pelin Kaytmaz, Noureddine Khaous, Charbel Kindji, Meriam Maadi, Abdoulaye Mbaye, Claire Perroux, Isma\"el Rousseau, Papa S\'ega Wad\'e, Gilles Xiberras, Olivier Zhang, Malek Zitouni
data.summary: Wolof is spoken by 23M people, mostly in Senegal, but remains weakly supported by open-weight language models, while API models raise cost, governance, and sovereignty constraints for local deployments. In this paper, we present 0.6B-14B open-weight models adapted to Wolof through instruction tuning, preference alignment, and model merging. After presenting the pipeline and data, extensive experiments on 63~public and in-house tasks show good performance on Wolof understanding and generation while remaining effective on other languages and cross-lingual skills, with the 8B and 14B models being particularly competitive with substantially larger commercial systems. The models are currently being evaluated in internal customer-care pilots and are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/collections/Orange/wolof-lm .

data.title: Recursive Semantic Divergence for LLM Agent Consistency
data.author: Harshavardhan Abichandani, Penny Chong, Atin Ghosh, Daniel Dahlmeier
data.summary: Large Language Model (LLM) agents with tool use can behave inconsistently across independent runs from identical states. They may call different tools, produce contradictory outputs, or follow divergent strategies. This variability compounds over time and undermines deployment reliability. Existing evaluation metrics primarily measure task correctness via completion-based scores and do not capture consistency in agent behavior across executions. Separately, agent behavior is analyzed either at the token level using probability distributions or at the single-response level using semantic clustering, but neither captures how inconsistency propagates across future turns of a trajectory. We introduce Recursive Semantic Divergence (RSD), a trajectory-level consistency metric adapted from bisimulation metrics in reinforcement learning. RSD measures the expected cumulative semantic disagreement between two independent rollouts of the same agent from the same state, using natural language inference to detect logical inconsistency. It is defined recursively over future states and approximated by a neural network trained on independent rollouts. The learned metric estimates future divergence from the current state, providing a consistency score at each turn without requiring the full trajectory to complete. When used as a reward signal for fine-tuning, RSD reduces AUC coefficient of variation (CV) by up to 30.9% on tau2-bench and 50.5% on ToolSandbox. Across Qwen-2.5 and Qwen-3.5 models, RSD reduces AUC CV in seven out of eight model-benchmark settings, while improving the final task progress in all eight settings.

data.title: Examining form-based linguistic productivity in people and large language models
data.author: Michael Wilson, Robert Frank
data.summary: Linguistic productivity, as evidenced by the use of words in novel contexts, is one of the most striking facts about human language. However, how abstract the knowledge that enables such productivity is remains unclear. We compare people's and computational language models' linguistic productivity in contexts where successful generalization depends on form-based information. We focus on extending the use of a novel verb learned in the active voice to passive contexts. We find people extend active to passive uses in a way consistent with abstract generalizations concerning linguistic form, even when no plausible meaning can be assigned to the novel verb. In contrast, large language models succeeded only when a meaning like an existing verb's could be assigned to the novel verb. We conclude that computational models' syntactic knowledge remains tied to the distribution and meaning of specific lexical items in a way that human syntactic knowledge is not.

data.title: Style over Substance? Linguistic Bias in LLM-based Peer Review
data.author: Sai Suresh Macharla Vasu, Sumedh Santosh Joshi, Philipp Christmann, Ivaxi Sheth, Ruta Binkyte, Koel Dutta Chowdhury, Raouf Kerkouche, Hui-Po Wang, Mario Fritz
data.summary: The number of paper submissions to major AI conferences has increased dramatically in recent years, substantially increasing the peer-review workload of researchers. At the same time, large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to support peer review, both by individual reviewers and by conference organizations. While LLM capabilities have improved considerably, their evaluations may be influenced by linguistic characteristics that are unrelated to scientific content. In this work, we introduce a controlled experimental framework for studying such effects by systematically perturbing the linguistic style of research papers. Specifically, we rewrite papers to exhibit (i) linguistic features associated with native or non-native English writing, and (ii) high- or low-confidence linguistic features. To construct these interventions, we derive fine-grained rewriting instructions grounded in the linguistic literature and apply them using LLMs. Crucially, our interventions are designed to preserve the underlying scientific content. We then evaluate the resulting papers using different LLM reviewers. Our experiments expose a critical vulnerability in LLM-based peer review: reviewers systematically reward confident rhetoric independent of scientific content, raising serious concerns about the robustness of their assessments.

oai:arXiv.org:2610.35254v3.label: Style over Substance? Linguistic Bias in LLM-based Peer Review

data.title: CAMR: Compatibility-Aware Memory Replay for Continual Learning in Large Language Models
data.author: Jingpu Yang, Tianhao Li, Fengxian Ji, Yufeng Wang, Shuxin Zheng, Xiaoqing Zhang
data.summary: Continual learning requires large language models to acquire new knowledge and capabilities while retaining what they have learned. Fine-tuning and replay support acquisition and retention, but deciding whether incoming examples need supervision and which historical examples to revisit remains a challenge. We propose Compatibility-Aware Memory Replay (CAMR), an adaptive framework that jointly controls current-example supervision and historical replay. CAMR combines compatibility checks with a learned memory gate to guide an online policy over three actions: learning incoming examples with general replay, jointly reinforcing compatible related examples, and skipping direct supervision of verified mastered duplicates. The policy learns from acquisition, retention, and training-cost feedback under a bounded per-arrival replay budget. We evaluate CAMR with Qwen3-8B-Base on continual factual updating and cross-task and cross-domain learning. On WikiBigEdit, CAMR consistently leads evaluated methods in Original Match from 3K to 100K facts, reaching 93.66% after just 3K facts and surpassing Full-history Replay (LoRA) after 100K facts. It also achieves the highest final scores on all four selected TRACE tasks and maintains or improves earlier-task performance relative to post-acquisition levels in a sequence spanning financial question answering, mathematical reasoning, code generation, and summarization.

data.title: In-Model Context Compression with Agentic Soft Tokens for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
data.author: Xuning He, Kai Fan, Runyu Zhang, Binghuan Wang, Yuxiang Zhang, Xue Jiang, Yihong Dong
data.summary: Long-horizon LLM agents play an important role in solving complex and sustained tasks, with ever-growing interaction contexts. However, these accumulated contexts will raise substantial computational cost and obscure key decision-relevant evidence. Existing methods typically train external compressors or context-management agents to rewrite context as shorter hard-token sequences, but such external selection may not align with the LLM's evolving representation and is necessarily lossy. In this paper, we introduce Agentic Soft-Token Compression (ASTC), a training-free compression method using soft tokens within LLM agent for long-horizon tasks. Specifically, ASTC uses the model's native recurrent dynamics to determine the already absorbed information, leveraging the commonly-used hybrid Gated Delta Network (GDN)-attention. It then carries this information forward as agentic soft tokens while retaining exact values as hard tokens. The resulting compact sequence reduces later-layer computation and yields reusable KV caches, extending the savings across the agent's trajectory. Extensive experiments on long-horizon tasks show that ASTC matches or exceeds the uncompressed agent's accuracy with up to 59.84% fewer end-to-end Attention Pairs, while trained compressors require 12.3 to 194.9 times more Attention Pairs per successful task. These findings highlight agentic soft tokens as a model-native way to carry absorbed context forward as the task representation evolves.

data.title: CardioLM: A multilingual suite of small language models for the cardiology domain
data.author: Manuela-Daniela Danu, Miguel Rodr\'iguez-Ortega, Alberto Becerra-Tome, Pablo Arancibia, Fernando Gallego-Donoso, Lorenzo Pratesi, Xi Bai, Andrei-Damian Dinescu, Salvador Lima-L\'opez, Andrea Guala, Saskia Haitjema, Jonas Mack, Michele Miranda, Wesam Al Nabki, Jan Rodr\'iguez-Miret, Vasile George Marica, Vladim\'ir Kincl, Kate\v{r}ina Dost\'alov\'a, Michael Andrej, Alicia Ujil, Corinne Allaart, Machteld Boonstra, Malin Overmars, Anoop Shah, Giovanna Ceroni, Jonathan Kossoff, Domenico D'Amario, Renzo Laborante, Antonio Iaconelli, Isabella Fumarulo, Jacopo Lenkowicz, Livia Lilli, Emma Weiss, Alex Scafa, Felix Lindberg, Milou Gamage, Eul\`alia Farr\'e-Maduell, S\'ebastien Brati\`eres, Martin Krallinger, Bram van Es
data.summary:
Background: Cardiovascular care generates large volumes of clinical free-text documentation in local languages. However, clinical natural language processing (NLP) resources remain concentrated in English, and no existing benchmark is cardiology-specific, multilingual, and broad in entity coverage.
Methods: We present two contributions. The first is CardioCCC, a corpus of 508 cardiology case reports originally published in Spanish and extended to Czech, Dutch, English, Italian, Romanian, and Swedish through machine translation, annotation projection, and clinician review, with annotations covering diseases, symptoms, procedures, and medications. The second is CardioLM, comprising CardioBERTa, a set of language-specific encoders obtained by continued pretraining on cardiology and biomedical corpora, and CardioNER, a set of named entity recognition (NER) models fine-tuned on CardioCCC.
Results: Cardiology-specific pretraining reduced pseudo-perplexity by up to a factor of eight, yet changed strict span-level F1 by at most 0.04, with benefits concentrated in languages whose backbones lacked biomedical coverage. The jointly trained multilingual XLM-RoBERTa-large models achieved the best strict F1 in nearly every language and entity type, exceeding the strongest monolingual system by up to 0.13 F1. A large share of residual errors concerned boundary detection: relaxed matching recovered 0.10-0.23 F1 for disease, procedure, and symptom, but only 0.01-0.07 for medication. Clinicians rated CardioNER well above a rule- and dictionary-based baseline, with the mean rating across entity types rising from 26% to 73%.
Conclusions: Specialty-specific pretraining is not the decisive factor for downstream entity recognition, whereas multilingual joint training yields the strongest results in nearly all settings and a simpler deployment path for multi-country clinical information extraction.

data.title: Beyond Truncation: When Can LLMs Safely Omit Generated Text?
data.author: Mahmoud Alyosify, Mirna Imbabi, Eman Elkhamisi, Rahatara Ferdousi
data.summary: Instruction-tuned large language models (LLMs) answer at greater length than a request needs. We ask whether a training-free controller inside the decoding loop can remove that surplus while preserving content, judged against the simplest possible baseline: truncating the model's own answer to the same length. An entropy-gated logits processor removes 25.5-34.9% of tokens on MT-Bench development questions and 19.9-34.2% on a sealed test split within pre-registered BERTScore non-inferiority margins, yet we prove and confirm by audit that its output is always a prefix of the unmodified answer: the saving is truncation. A survey of 23 training-free mechanism families finds none that selects content better than truncation without oracle labels. We therefore introduce Entailment-Licensed In-Decoding Elision (ELIDE), which, at each sentence boundary, withholds a span from the reader only when a natural-language inference model judges it entailed by the text already shown, while leaving the model's generation unchanged. ELIDE beats matched-length truncation on three model families, but reading 936 of its elisions on 670 public prompts shows that 59% harm the answer, a failure that no automatic measure detects. Scoping the licence to its discourse unit reduces the harmful share to about one elision in ten on two fresh tests.

oai:arXiv.org:2611.08975v2.label: Beyond Truncation: When Can LLMs Safely Omit Generated Text?

data.title: A Closer Look at Language Model Introspection: Probing Information and Reporting
data.author: Dustin Rubin, Vincenzo Timmel, Xufeng He, Aritra Saha, JooMan Kim, Vijay Madisetti
data.summary: One way to study language-model introspection is to test whether models can identify where their activations have been perturbed. We train a simple linear classifier to identify the perturbed sentence from the model's activations, then compare its predictions with the model's own answers across pretraining and injection strengths. This tests whether the model is being asked to report information that is already easy to recover. If so, successful localization may be less demanding than it first appears and may not extend to the broader uses that motivate introspection research, such as faithfully explaining a model's reasoning or helping researchers assess the reliability of its answers. With an injection four times the typical activation norm at layer 0 and probe readout at layer 24 in OLMo 3 32B, the supervised probe reaches 98.3 % accuracy after 8.4 billion training tokens, while the model's zero-shot answer remains at chance (11.1 %). At the released base checkpoint, these accuracies reach 99.1 % and 89.6 %, respectively. Across 7B and 32B, location is already decodable in randomly initialized networks, showing that the architecture can support these traces without pretraining. In these experiments, location information lies close enough to the surface for a simple linear probe to recover it, so successful reporting need not imply broader access to the model's internal computation.

oai:arXiv.org:2611.15267v2.label: A Closer Look at Language Model Introspection: Probing Information and Reporting

data.title: GT-FENG: General Theory of Factual Evaluation and Normative Grounding in Language Models
data.author: Jiayu Feng
data.summary: Whether a language model's answer is correct often depends on context: the same value can be right under one jurisdiction, date, or legal definition and wrong under another. We introduce GT-FENG (General Theory of Factual Evaluation and Normative Grounding), the first general framework to unify contextual/temporal correctness and rule-based error attribution across law, policy, and other rule-governed domains. GT-FENG checks answers against the applicable rules and identifies documented rules that match incorrect answers. It shows that when multiple rules give the same value, the answer alone cannot tell which rule the model used. In Medicaid income-limit answers from two models, documenting the asked state's own records reduces the number of wrong answers that match only other states' values by 68-78%, and more than half of stable wrong answers then match two or more documented sources. GT-FENG provides a foundation for evaluating language models in rule-governed domains and for future benchmarks and evaluation toolkits. We release GT-FENG as an open-source Python package, gtfeng.

oai:arXiv.org:2611.18279v2.label: GT-FENG: General Theory of Factual Evaluation and Normative Grounding in Language Models

data.title: ResBench: Benchmarking LLM-Generated FPGA Designs with Resource Awareness
data.author: Ce Guo, Tong Zhao
data.summary: Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs) are widely used in modern hardware design, yet writing Hardware Description Language (HDL) code for FPGA implementation remains a complex and time-consuming task. Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as a promising tool for HDL generation, but existing benchmarks for LLM-based code generation primarily focus on functional correctness while overlooking hardware resource usage. Furthermore, current benchmarks offer limited diversity and do not fully represent the wide range of real-world FPGA applications. To address these shortcomings, we introduce ResBench, the first resource-focused benchmark explicitly designed to distinguish between resource-optimized and inefficient LLM-generated HDL code. ResBench consists of 56 problems across 12 categories, covering applications from finite state machines to financial computing. Our open-source evaluation framework automatically tests LLMs by generating Verilog code, verifying correctness, and measuring resource usage. The experiments, which primarily analyze Lookup Table (LUT) usage, reveal significant differences among LLMs, demonstrating ResBench's capability to identify models that generate more resource-optimized FPGA designs.

oai:arXiv.org:2503.08823v3.label: ResBench: Benchmarking LLM-Generated FPGA Designs with Resource Awareness

data.title: BitBypass: A New Direction in Jailbreaking Aligned Large Language Models with Bitstream Camouflage
data.author: Kalyan Nakka, Nitesh Saxena
data.summary: The inherent risk of generating harmful and unsafe content by Large Language Models (LLMs), has highlighted the need for their safety alignment. Various techniques like supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning from human feedback, and red-teaming were developed for ensuring the safety alignment of LLMs. However, the robustness of these aligned LLMs is always challenged by adversarial attacks that exploit unexplored and underlying vulnerabilities of the safety alignment. In this paper, we develop a novel black-box jailbreak attack, called BitBypass, that leverages hyphen-separated bitstream camouflage for jailbreaking aligned LLMs. This represents a new direction in jailbreaking by exploiting fundamental information representation of data as continuous bits, rather than leveraging prompt engineering or adversarial manipulations. Our evaluation of five state-of-the-art LLMs, namely GPT-4o, Gemini 1.5, Claude 3.5, Llama 3.1, and Mixtral, in adversarial perspective, revealed the capabilities of BitBypass in bypassing their safety alignment and tricking them into generating harmful and unsafe content. Further, we observed that BitBypass outperforms several state-of-the-art jailbreak attacks in terms of stealthiness and attack success. Overall, these results highlights the effectiveness and efficiency of BitBypass in jailbreaking these state-of-the-art LLMs.

oai:arXiv.org:2506.02479v3.label: BitBypass: A New Direction in Jailbreaking Aligned Large Language Models with Bitstream Camouflage

data.title: SmartThinker: Learning High-Density Reasoning via Step-Level Token Allocation
data.author: Xingyang He, Xiao Ling, Jie Liu
data.summary: Large reasoning models (LRMs) have exhibited remarkable reasoning capabilities through inference-time scaling, but this progress has also introduced considerable redundancy and inefficiency into their reasoning processes, resulting in substantial computational waste. Previous work has attempted to mitigate this issue by penalizing the overall length of generated samples during reinforcement learning (RL), with the goal of encouraging a more concise chains of Efficient reasoning is critical for large reasoning models (LRMs) deployed in agent systems with strict context constraints. Existing methods predominantly rely on global length penalties that overlook step-level structure, inadvertently compressing critical derivations while retaining low-value detours. Hence, we argue for a principled, step-aware alternative that preserves critical steps and compresses low-value detours. However, it raises three fundamental challenges: the difficulty of obtaining step-level supervision, the need for reward signals that induce differentiated length pressure, and the requirement to balance training stability with exploration on complex problems. We propose SmartThinker, a step-level token allocation framework that learns to selectively preserve or compress individual reasoning steps. At its core is Step-Level Length Control Policy Optimization (SCPO), which provides label-free feedback by online estimation of each step's contribution from the change in correct-answer likelihood after removing it. We further introduce reasoning density, defined as contribution per token, to relax length pressure on high-value steps while intensifying it on low-density ones. Finally, SCPO stabilizes training through length-bias-corrected advantages and difficulty-adaptive clipping, achieving superior accuracy-efficiency trade-offs across nine in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks.

oai:arXiv.org:2507.04348v3.label: SmartThinker: Learning High-Density Reasoning via Step-Level Token Allocation

data.title: Toward LLM-Supported Automated Assessment of Critical Thinking Subskills
data.author: Marisa C. Peczuh, Nischal Ashok Kumar, Ryan Baker, Blair Lehman, Danielle Eisenberg, Caitlin Mills, Payu Wittawatolarn, Kushaan Naskar, Keerthi Chebrolu, Sudhip Nashi, Cadence Young, Brayden Liu, Sherry Lachman, Andrew Lan
data.summary: As the world becomes increasingly saturated with AI-generated content, disinformation, and algorithmic persuasion, critical thinking - the capacity to evaluate evidence, detect unreliable claims, and exercise independent judgment - is becoming a defining human skill. Developing critical thinking skills through timely assessment and feedback is crucial; however, there has not been extensive work in educational data mining on defining, measuring, and supporting critical thinking. In this paper, we investigate the feasibility of measuring "subskills" that underlie critical thinking. We ground our work in an authentic task where students operationalize critical thinking by writing argumentative essays. We developed a coding rubric based on an established skills progression and completed human coding for a corpus of student essays. We then evaluated three distinct approaches to automated scoring: zero-shot prompting, few-shot prompting, and supervised fine-tuning, implemented across three large language models (GPT-5, Llama 3.1 8B, and ModernBERT). Fine-tuning Llama 3.1 8B achieved the best results and demonstrated particular strength on subskills with highly separable proficiency levels with balanced labels across levels, while lower performance was observed for subskills that required detection of subtle distinctions between proficiency levels or imbalanced labels. Our exploratory work represents an initial step toward scalable assessment of critical thinking skills across authentic educational contexts. Future research should continue to combine automated critical thinking assessment with human validation to more accurately detect and measure dynamic, higher-order thinking skills.

oai:arXiv.org:2510.12915v3.label: Toward LLM-Supported Automated Assessment of Critical Thinking Subskills

data.title: Fidelity Before Structure: Verbatim Chunks Beat Lossy Artifact Extraction in Long-Conversation LLM Memory
data.author: Tao An
data.summary: A growing class of conversational-memory systems compresses dialogue history into structured artifacts (extracted facts, decisions, or events). The premise is that distilled structure retrieves better than raw text. We test this premise with a controlled ablation. Within one fixed retrieval--rerank--reasoning pipeline, we swap only the stored representation (LLM-extracted typed artifacts versus verbatim conversation chunks) and hold the model, retriever, reranker, and judge constant. Verbatim chunks win by 15.9 points on LoCoMo (43.9% vs. 28.0%) and by 22.0 points on LongMemEval-S (67.4% vs. 45.4%). A semantic graph does not recover the gap, and six confound controls reproduce the effect. The mechanism is lossy distillation rather than structure per se. Accuracy tracks how much source text survives in the store, and the extracted-artifact pipeline does not beat naive RAG in overall accuracy (chunks do abstain worse; see Limitations). For the extraction designs we test, structured memory should augment verbatim text rather than replace it. Adding artifacts alongside chunks costs no detected accuracy, while substituting them forfeits the gap. Code and data are available at https://github.com/tao-hpu/cog-canvas.

oai:arXiv.org:2601.00821v5.label: Fidelity Before Structure: Verbatim Chunks Beat Lossy Artifact Extraction in Long-Conversation LLM Memory

data.title: TERMINATOR: Learning Optimal Exit Points for Early Stopping in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
data.author: Alliot Nagle, Jakhongir Saydaliev, Dhia Garbaya, Michael Gastpar, Ashok Vardhan Makkuva, Hyeji Kim
data.summary: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) achieve impressive performance on complex reasoning tasks via Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, which enables them to generate intermediate thinking tokens before arriving at the final answer. However, LRMs often suffer from significant overthinking, spending excessive compute time even after the answer is generated early on. Prior work has identified the existence of an optimal reasoning length such that truncating reasoning at this point significantly shortens CoT outputs with virtually no change in performance. However, determining optimal CoT lengths for practical datasets is highly non-trivial as they are fully task and model-dependent. In this paper, we precisely address this and design Terminator, an early-exit strategy for LRMs at inference to mitigate overthinking. The central idea underpinning Terminator is that the first arrival of an LRM's final answer is often predictable, and we leverage these first answer positions to create a novel dataset of optimal reasoning lengths to train Terminator. Powered by this approach, Terminator achieves significant reductions in CoT lengths of 14%-55% on average across four challenging practical datasets: MATH-500, AIME 2025, HumanEval, and GPQA, while outperforming current state-of-the-art methods and reducing inference latency by more than 2x compared to the original LRM.Project page: https://terminator-llm.github.io

oai:arXiv.org:2603.12529v3.label: TERMINATOR: Learning Optimal Exit Points for Early Stopping in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning

data.title: Automated Code Efficiency Optimization via Agent Skill Mining
data.author: Zimu Wang, Yuling Shi, Mengfan Li, Zijun Liu, Jie M. Zhang, Chengcheng Wan, Xiaodong Gu
data.summary: Code efficiency is a fundamental aspect of software quality, yet how to use large language models (LLMs) to optimize correct programs remains challenging. Prior approaches rely on one-shot rewriting, retrieved exemplars or instructions, fine-tuning, or candidate search. In this paper, we present EffiSkill, a two-stage framework that models recurring slow-to-fast transformations as Operator Skills: persistent cards that record a transformation's intent, applicability, procedure, expected effect, and risks. Stage I distills frozen, language-specific skill libraries from slow/fast program pairs. Stage II diagnoses a new program, retrieves relevant skills, composes alternative plans, and generates up to eight candidates. These steps finish without candidate-execution feedback; public tests then filter and rank candidates, and held-out private tests determine reported correctness and speedup. Across 623 EffiBench-X tasks per language, two backbones, and separate Python and C++ evaluations, EffiSkill achieves the highest observed OPT@1 and OPT@8 among the compared methods in all four settings. Its OPT@8 margins over the strongest baselines range from 4.98 to 12.52 percentage points. These results support broader successful optimization coverage for the complete skill-guided pipeline under a shared output budget.

oai:arXiv.org:2603.27850v2.label: Automated Code Efficiency Optimization via Agent Skill Mining

data.title: ORACLE-SWE: Quantifying the Contribution of Critical Information Signals on SWE Agents
data.author: Kenan Li, Qirui Jin, Liao Zhu, Xiaosong Huang, Yijia Wu, Yikai Zhang, Xin Zhang, Zijian Jin, Yufan Huang, Elsie Nallipogu, Chaoyun Zhang, Yu Kang, Saravan Rajmohan, Qingwei Lin, Wenke Lee, Dongmei Zhang
data.summary: Recent advances in Language Model (LM) agents have increasingly focused on repository-level software engineering (SWE) tasks, leading to various agentic workflows, training methods and failure analysis. Interestingly, rather than directly generating or evaluating edit patches, these approaches first examine and improve intermediate information signals collected during agent exploration, including Reproduction Test, Regression Test, Edit Location, Execution Context, and API Usage. Although different studies examine different subsets of these signals, no work has systematically compared their relative effectiveness in improving final task success or measured the remaining space for improvement in each signal. To address this gap, this work quantifies the contributions of both oracle and agent-extracted signals to final task success and measures the gap between current agent-found signals and their oracle counterparts. We hope our findings could suggest future research emphasis in SWE agents. We release our source code and oracle-signal dataset as a reusable methodology to benefit future signal analysis of SWE agents.

oai:arXiv.org:2604.07789v4.label: ORACLE-SWE: Quantifying the Contribution of Critical Information Signals on SWE Agents

data.title: The Granularity Axis: A Micro-to-Macro Latent Direction for Social Roles in Language Models
data.author: Chonghan Qin, Xiachong Feng, Ziyun Song, Xiaocheng Feng, Jing Xiong, Lingpeng Kong
data.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are prompted to adopt social roles from individuals to institutions, but whether their representations encode this difference in social granularity remains unclear. We discover a contrast-based Granularity Axis, the difference between mean macro- and micro-role hidden states, that aligns with the dominant geometry of role space: in Qwen3-8B, its cosine with PC1 is $0.972$, and PC1 explains $52.6\%$ of the variance. Across 75 roles at five levels, with 90,000 role-conditioned and 1,200 default responses per model, projections increase monotonically and remain stable across layers, prompts, and response-quality filters. The structure transfers to Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and scales to Qwen3-32B and Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct, whose PC1 shares are $45.99\%$ and $31.23\%$. Independent five-rater validation ($\alpha=0.961$) preserves the ordering; identical continuations and affect/formality controls confirm scale-related variation beyond generated wording. The axis is also behaviorally causal: positive steering moves Llama from $2.00$ to $3.17$ on a five-point macro scale for prompts admitting local responses. Steering strength and stability depend on the model's default operating regime. Together, these findings establish social granularity as a representational primitive: a continuous, ordered, causally manipulable direction organizing role-conditioned generation across model families.

oai:arXiv.org:2605.06196v2.label: The Granularity Axis: A Micro-to-Macro Latent Direction for Social Roles in Language Models

data.title: LatentRouter: Can We Choose the Right Multimodal Large Language Model Before Seeing Its Answer?
data.author: Xueqi Cheng, Yushun Dong
data.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have heterogeneous strengths across OCR, chart understanding, spatial reasoning, visual question answering, cost, and latency. Effective MLLM routing therefore requires more than estimating query difficulty: a router must match the multimodal requirements of the current image-question input with the capabilities of each candidate model. We propose LatentRouter, a router that formulates MLLM routing as counterfactual multimodal utility prediction. Given an image-question query, LatentRouter extracts learned multimodal routing capsules, represents each candidate MLLM with a model capability token, and performs latent communication between these states to estimate how each model would perform if selected. A distributional outcome head predicts model-specific counterfactual quality, while a bounded capsule correction refines close decisions without allowing residual signals to dominate the prediction. The resulting utility-based policy supports performance-oriented and performance-cost routing, and handles changing candidate pools through shared per-model scoring with availability masking. Experiments on MMR-Bench and VL-RouterBench show that LatentRouter outperforms fixed-model, feature-level, and learned-router baselines. Additional analyses show that the gains are strongest on multimodal task groups where model choice depends on visual, layout-sensitive, or reasoning-oriented requirements, and that latent communication is the main contributor to the improvement. The code is available at: https://github.com/LabRAI/LatentRouter.

oai:arXiv.org:2605.11301v2.label: LatentRouter: Can We Choose the Right Multimodal Large Language Model Before Seeing Its Answer?

data.title: HEED: Density-Weighted Residual Alignment for Hybrid Vision-Language Model Distillation
data.author: Yihao Liang, Niraj K. Jha
data.summary: Distilling vision-language models into faster hybrid architectures, such as 3:1 Mamba-2/attention mixes, is now standard practice for making inference efficient. Aggregate benchmarks suggest that this works but they hide selective failures. When we distill Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct into a 3:1 Mamba-2/attention hybrid, student model stays within 2 points of the teacher across visual reasoning benchmarks like MMStar, MMBench, and MMMU-Pro, while dropping 13 points on optical-character-recognition and document tasks. The student can still understand the scene but loses the fine-grained text needed to answer. We localize much of the failure to a specific kind of position. In a high-resolution image, most patches are sky, wall, or smooth texture, while a small fraction carries text, edges, object boundaries, or other local details. In a token-level diagnostic, the top 10% highest-density patches have 3.6x larger residual drift than the bottom 10% lowest-density patches and 3.5x larger teacher-masking answer contribution. Uniform weighting devotes many loss terms to low-information background patches, whereas sparse answer bearing patches receive no special protection. The required intervention is minimal: we replace uniform residual alignment with density-weighted residual alignment, using patch self-dissimilarity as a training-free proxy for position importance. We call this HEED. Compared with normal end-to-end distillation, HEED increases performance by 8.7 points on OCRBench v2 and 5.13 points on a 10-benchmark average. The gain is realized on different teacher models. After standard post-training, the student reaches teacher-level performance on the 10-benchmark average. HEED adds no parameters and no inference-time cost. Hence, the student maintains the hybrid architecture's 4.12x throughput and 68% memory saving at 128k context. Code is available at https://github.com/jha-lab/HEED.

data.title: AI Agents May Always Fall for Prompt Injections
data.author: Sahar Abdelnabi, Eugene Bagdasarian
data.summary: Prompt injection is the most critical vulnerability in deployed AI agents. Despite recent progress, we show that the prevailing defense paradigm (data-instruction separation) both fails to detect attacks that operate through contextual manipulation and degrades contextually appropriate behavior. We then recast prompt injection via the lens of Contextual Integrity (CI), a privacy theory that judges information flow compliance with contextual norms. This explains types of attacks that current defenses attempt to patch and predict advanced ones future agents will face. We develop unique benign and attack scenarios that force an agent to violate the norms by (1) misrepresenting the flow, (2) manipulating norms, or (3) mixing multiple flows. This reframing suggests an impossibility argument: an adversary can always construct a context under which a blocked flow appears legitimate, or a defender who tightens norms will block genuinely legitimate flows. Our findings suggest that current research addresses a shrinking fraction of future attack surfaces. Instead, through CI, we offer a principled framework for evaluating context-sensitive failures, and designing CI-aware alignment for frontier autonomous agents.

oai:arXiv.org:2605.17634v2.label: AI Agents May Always Fall for Prompt Injections

data.title: Do Coding Agents Deceive Us? Detecting and Preventing Cheating via Capped Evaluation with Randomized Tests
data.author: Thanawat Lodkaew, Johannes Ackermann, Soichiro Nishimori, Nontawat Charoenphakdee, Masashi Sugiyama, Takashi Ishida
data.summary: A growing failure mode in agent evaluation and training is that models can achieve high evaluation scores (e.g., test pass rates) by exploiting shortcuts instead of solving the intended task, making these scores deceptive. This makes evaluation scores unreliable as measures of true task-solving ability. We propose CapCode, a framework for constructing coding datasets with randomized tests whose best achievable non-cheating score is deliberately capped below 100%. This capped-score design gives evaluation scores a clearer interpretation: scores substantially above the cap are implausible and therefore provide evidence of cheating. To prevent cheating, we propose CapReward, a reward design based on the CapCode principle to discourage optimization beyond the cap. Experiments across multiple datasets show that CapCode detects cheating while preserving performance ranking of models, and CapReward reduces cheating behavior, yielding models that better follow the intended task specification.

data.title: RAS: Measuring LLM Safety Through Refusal Alignment
data.author: Chang-Chieh Huang, Yan-Lun Chen, Chia-Mu Yu, Wei-Bin Lee
data.summary: Repeated safety evaluation of open-weight large language models requires generating and judging responses for many related checkpoints. We introduce RAS (Refusal Alignment Score), a representation-based, reference-relative indicator of harmful-request refusal computed by the five-stage SafeVec procedure. SafeVec extracts layer-wise refusal directions from an aligned reference model, measures their alignment in related targets, and calibrates a score from 0 to 100 using behavioral attack success rates (ASR) from reference and calibration models. Subsequent target scoring uses input forward passes alone. Across 18 held-out variants from the Llama, Gemma, and Qwen families, RAS correlates with $100(1-\mathrm{ASR})$ (Pearson 0.934, Spearman 0.851) and achieves 83.0% pairwise ordering agreement. Across five prompt configurations for the Llama reference, directions have mean cosine similarity 0.939. With calibration ASR already available, setup-inclusive evaluation of five targets achieves a speedup of 3.2 to 80.5 times over the specified behavioral protocol. These results support refusal alignment as an efficient signal for screening related checkpoints and prioritizing behavioral audits.

data.title: Cited Web Sources in LLM Answers about Brands: A Multilingual Audit
data.author: Dmitrij \.Zatuchin
data.summary: Displayed citations make part of generative search observable, but they do not reveal its complete retrieval process. This audit covers three archived datasets containing 167,551 URL-bearing citation entries across 128 brands, 13 languages and 12 home markets. In the principal Nordic-Baltic component, 3,863 of 21,033 registrable domains account for 80% of 131,514 citations. Wikipedia leads in 11 of 12 query languages. A recovered, separate brand-associated website classification retains 131,512 entries: 108,410 (82.4%) fall outside its brand-associated category and 23,102 (17.6%) inside. This classification does not establish legal ownership. In the full 57-brand Polish aggregate, four recruitment hosts receive 637 citations against 297 for Polish Wikipedia. The results show why normalization, classification rules and denominators belong in citation audits. They describe displayed links without estimating causal effects on brand reputation.

data.title: From Weights to Features: Sparse-Autoencoder-Guided Activation Regularization for Continual Learning in Large Language Models
data.author: Evan Ning, Wei Xue, Dong Lou, Yike Guo
data.summary: Weight-protecting regularizers such as elastic weight consolidation (EWC) are a standard defense against catastrophic forgetting; however, in the sequential fine-tuning of large language models, they exhibit a stability-plasticity tradeoff that penalty tuning cannot resolve. We attribute this limitation in part to polysemanticity: because each weight participates in many unrelated concepts, a per-weight importance score has difficulty isolating the knowledge that requires protection. We instead regularize in activation space, using a pretrained sparse autoencoder (SAE) as a fixed dictionary of approximately monosemantic features. We formulate continual learning as constrained optimization over feature drift, with a stability constraint on the features to be preserved and a plasticity constraint on the features used by the current task, and we show that the resulting squared-hinge loss is a regularized Lagrangian relaxation of this problem, with EWC as a special case. A replay variant measures drift on 200 stored sequences per previous task, whereas a data-free variant stores only a 197 KB feature mask per task, versus 6.5 GB for EWC. On TRACE (Gemma-2 9B, Llama-3.1 8B) and MedCL (Gemma-2 9B), the replay variant matches or exceeds SAE-based feature distillation at approximately one third of its per-step cost, and the data-free variant attains the highest mean overall performance among methods that store no previous-task data and add no task-specific parameters. Task-relevant units are linearly separable in the SAE basis but not in the neuron basis (ROC-AUC of 0.87-0.88 versus 0.50), and weight-space protection constrains the features of other tasks nearly as strongly as those of the protected task.

oai:arXiv.org:2606.26629v2.label: From Weights to Features: Sparse-Autoencoder-Guided Activation Regularization for Continual Learning in Large Language Models

data.title: Multi-Head Recurrent Memory Agents
data.author: Jiatong Li, Samuel Yeh, Sharon Li
data.summary: Recurrent memory agents extend LLMs to arbitrarily long contexts by iteratively consolidating input into a fixed-size memory window. Despite their scalability, these agents exhibit a well-documented reliability problem: end-to-end performance degrades systematically as context length grows. We diagnose this failure by decomposing performance into two factors---memory capture and memory retention---and quantitatively confirm that retention is the dominant bottleneck. Retention collapses because existing designs maintain memory as a monolithic text block, forcing every update to risk overwriting previously retained content. Motivated by this diagnosis, we propose Multi-Head Recurrent Memory (MHM), a general, training-free framework that partitions memory into independent heads governed by a stage-wise select-then-update strategy. At each step, exactly one head is selected for update while the remaining heads are structurally shielded from overwriting, shifting the burden of retention from model behavior to architectural design. As a lightweight instantiation, we introduce Least-Recently-Updated MHM (MHM-LRU), which guarantees uniform head utilization with zero additional token overhead. Extensive experiments on long-context benchmarks show that MHM-LRU substantially improves both retention and end-to-end accuracy across the 100K--1M token range, where baselines degrade sharply. On RULER-HQA at 896K tokens, MHM-LRU improves the memory retention rate from less than 30% to 73.96%. These gains generalize across model families, scales, and task types, positioning architectural optimization as a practical and cost-efficient path toward reliable long-context recurrent memory.

data.title: Change2Task: From Repository Changes to Executable Coding Agent Tasks and Environments
data.author: Haomin Qi, Xingliang Wang, Xuanqi Gao, Baihui Sang, Xin Zhang, Minghua Ma, Pengfei Gao, Yu Kang, Qingwei Lin, Saravan Rajmohan, Dongmei Zhang, Qi Zhang
data.summary: Coding agents learn from and are measured on executable tasks, but building such tasks from repository history usually means rebuilding an environment at an old revision for every task, which is costly and brittle. We observe that a merged pull request (PR) can instead be undone on today's code: removing the effect of a bug fix or feature from a maintained revision recreates the same task inside an environment that already builds and runs. We present Change2Task, which converts merged PRs into verified tasks on an up-to-date revision of the same repository. It reconstructs the pre-change state by patch reversal, code mapping, or agent-based rewriting, and keeps a task only if its target tests pass, fail, and pass again across the healthy, task, and restored states. From 1,130 PRs spanning bug fixing, feature addition, test generation, API migration, and security repair, Change2Task builds 900 verified tasks, recovering 29% more than SWE-smith's PR Mirror on matched bug-fix candidates. The reconstructed tasks preserve the evaluation signal: in aggregate, four coding agents solve 41.1% of tasks on both the original and reconstructed versions, with 89.7% per-task agreement. Sharing modern environments across tasks further reduces setup time by 58% and storage by 71%. On 11 private industrial repositories, Change2Task yields 1,000 tasks on which the strongest model reaches only 14.6% Pass@3.

oai:arXiv.org:2607.28591v3.label: Change2Task: From Repository Changes to Executable Coding Agent Tasks and Environments

data.title: A False Average: Pooled CoT-Monitor Accuracy Conceals a Reasoning-Dependent Fragility
data.author: Shikhar Shiromani, Leo Richter
data.summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitors are reported by their aggregate accuracy on a pool of reward hacks. We show that this number is a false average. On Terminal Wrench, about 77% of hacks are given away by the actions alone, and the monitor's pooled accuracy is dominated by them; on the remaining 23%, which an action-only monitor misses, the same monitor is fragile. We expose the fragility with a controlled attack: we rewrite only the agent's reasoning to read as good-faith engineering, leaving every command and output byte-identical. One gradient-free rewrite drops a held-out monitor's catch rate on that subset from about 95% to between 4 and 11%, while the pooled rate falls only about 25 points, near what the subset's share of the pool times its collapse predicts. The rewrite stays truthful about what happened and lies only about intent, so the trace-only monitors we test recover little, even when warned about the attack; of our defenses, only information from outside the trace helps much. The attack transfers across monitor and agent families, and the dataset's own hack labels show the same gradient with no monitor in the definition. Live agents told to hack on 27 tasks, with no monitor feedback, produce hollow hacks, but a monitor calibrated on each model's own honest solves catches nearly all of them. Applying the same rewrite to these live hacks keeps all 111 action-visible ones caught and lowers catch on the 16 whose actions score below 0.5 only from 16 to 13: the effect lands where the false average predicts, but the collapse stays a controlled result. A linear probe on a surrogate monitor's activations out-reads its verdict on the obfuscated hacks (AUC up to 0.98), but a behavioral control shows this edge does not, by itself, mean the monitor knows more than it says. Monitor accuracy should be reported on the reasoning-dependent subset, where the defense is load-bearing.

oai:arXiv.org:2608.00583v5.label: A False Average: Pooled CoT-Monitor Accuracy Conceals a Reasoning-Dependent Fragility

data.title: LangChoiceBench: Measuring and Explaining Programming-Language Choice in LLMs
data.author: Lukas Twist, Twm Stone, Helen Yannakoudakis, Jie M. Zhang
data.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to exhibit strong Python preferences when generating project-level code, but there is currently no systematic way to measure this behaviour across new models. To bridge this gap, we introduce LangChoiceBench, a project-level code-generation benchmark for measuring Python preference, recommendation-implementation consistency, and language diversity. LangChoiceBench covers 28 projects across seven software areas where Python is often a poor default. We evaluate 25 diverse LLMs and find that Python remains heavily over-selected, recommendation-implementation consistency is low, and smaller open-weight models generally show stronger Python preference and lower language diversity. We further analyse 9,826 reasoning traces and find that most Python choices are automatic or driven primarily by ease, rather than explicit consideration of project requirements. In a smaller but important set of cases, models fabricate contextual support for choosing Python - a failure mode we call phantom evidence - or produce code that contradicts the language selected in their own reasoning.

oai:arXiv.org:2608.06041v2.label: LangChoiceBench: Measuring and Explaining Programming-Language Choice in LLMs

data.title: How Diverse Are Layered Safeguards? Estimands and Measurement for Ensembles of LLM Jailbreak Defenses
data.author: Abrar Alotaibi, Moataz Ahmed
data.summary:
Practitioners protect large language models (LLMs) by stacking safeguards: a likelihood filter, a guard classifier, hidden-state probes, a decoding-time intervention. Such a stack is an ensemble of learned detectors, and ensemble theory states when combination pays: when members fail on different inputs. Stacking is recommended throughout the LLM security literature, but this condition has not been measured for any pair of safeguards.
The condition is three quantities, not one, and conflating them is why it has resisted measurement. Separately optimized attacks license only a claim about which \emph{behaviors} are jointly vulnerable; the identity that governs a deployed stack is written over shared \emph{inputs}; and neither predicts what an adversary attacking the assembled pipeline achieves. We define the three estimands, give an estimator for each, and supply two controls: the correlation between two independent runs of the same attack, which sets the level a pair must clear, and a multilevel model separating detector diversity from behavior difficulty.
On a seven-layer stack and two open-weight targets, no pair of safeguards is distinguishable from the correlation that two independent runs of the attack produce with no safeguard present, and behavior difficulty explains much of what remains. A second attack family, an attacker model rewriting its own prompts, reaches that verdict independently on a thirtieth of the budget and overturns the practical one: the only member that blocked the first adversary admits 0.19 under the second, against 0.03. Diversity between neural safeguards is measurable, but it and any member's strength are properties of a (stack, adversary, target) triple.

oai:arXiv.org:2608.28327v2.label: How Diverse Are Layered Safeguards? Estimands and Measurement for Ensembles of LLM Jailbreak Defenses

data.title: The Structure of Quantization Damage in LLMs: Why the Next Bit Should Be Spent Globally
data.author: Jundong Hu, Shekar Ramachandran
data.summary: Post-training quantization (PTQ) is widely used to reduce the cost of serving large language models (LLMs), but its accuracy cost is uneven and is often tuned per model. We study where quantization damage occurs and how to allocate a small additional precision budget. Using causal mixed-precision intervention as ground truth (raise each layer to 8-bit in turn and measure the accuracy it recovers) across 9 open-weight models in 4 architecture families, we test 3 intuitive hypotheses: that quantization damage lives in task circuits, where the model computes, or in weight statistics. None of them predicts which layers benefit from restored precision. Recovery is instead diffuse: for 8 of 9 models, recovering 75% of the gap takes roughly half the layers; the lone exception, Qwen3-8B, is sharply concentrated. At a matched precision budget, spending it globally on finer quantization granularity beats locally repairing the most recoverable layers for all 8 group-128-compatible models (all but OpenLLaMA, whose width rules out group-128), by 21-52 points, including the concentrated Qwen3-8B. We report 2 secondary findings: the residual is budget-limited (8-bit is near-lossless in our evaluation across RTN, GPTQ, and AWQ), and the location of peak recovery correlates with architecture within a family, though not across families. Within this budget setting, global granularity is a better default than selectively protecting critical layers. More broadly, cheap signals that correlate with quantization damage do not necessarily identify where restoring precision improves accuracy; this must be tested with causal intervention.

oai:arXiv.org:2609.01587v2.label: The Structure of Quantization Damage in LLMs: Why the Next Bit Should Be Spent Globally

data.title: Large Language Models Develop Belief State Geometry In-Context
data.author: Daniel Balcells, Andrew Jun Lee, Chirag Rastogi, Paul M. Riechers, Adam Shai, Xavier Poncini
data.summary: Large language models (LLMs) trained on next-token prediction exhibit remarkable in-context learning (ICL) abilities, yet the representations that support ICL remain poorly understood. We consider such representations in a controlled setting: prompting LLMs with data emitted from hidden Markov models (HMMs) and probing for the corresponding belief state -- the posterior distribution over the HMM's hidden states given the observed token history. Across six open-source LLMs prompted with data from 40 HMMs selected for non-trivial belief structure, we find that belief states are linearly decodable from residual stream activations, with peak probe $R^2$-values of 0.83-0.99 across HMM and LLM combinations, ranging from early to late layers. To establish functional relevance, we intervene directly on the probe-identified subspace via patching and steering, resulting in downstream prediction quality on the order of the untampered model, while controls degrade performance substantially. Together, these results provide representation-level evidence that ICL in open-source LLMs approximates optimal Bayesian prediction over a context-inferred generative model. More broadly, our findings extend prior results linking input-distribution structure to activation geometry: from toy networks trained explicitly on HMM data to production-scale LLMs.

oai:arXiv.org:2609.17376v2.label: Large Language Models Develop Belief State Geometry In-Context

data.title: Attribution Gaps in Zero-Training LLM+OVOD Pipelines: A Fine-Grained Analysis of the CAAP--SNAP Discrepancy
data.author: Yu-Feng Yen
data.summary: LAOD and similar zero-training LLM+open-vocabulary-detector (OVOD) pipelines score two things separately: class-agnostic localization accuracy (CAAP) and semantic naming accuracy (SNAP). The two consistently diverge, and nobody has asked why. This paper asks why, on the full 5,000-image COCO-Val split (27,273 detections) rather than the small subset the original work evaluated on. Object visual complexity turns out not to be the driver -- small and occluded objects are, if anything, localized better than large ones. Vocabulary novelty is: once the LLM's wording falls outside the detector's native category set, localization accuracy falls from 80.9% to 31.6%. That drop is not spread evenly across unfamiliar phrasing, though. Almost all of it comes from cases where the novel wording actually names a different object than the one COCO annotated (true synonyms still score 89.3%; semantically unrelated "noise" labels score 12.0%). A closer look at a further failure subset tells a similar story: 78-88% of what looks like complete localization failure is really the model correctly finding a real object that COCO's non-exhaustive 80-category scheme simply never labeled, not hallucination. Swap the detector backbone (YOLO-World for Grounding DINO) or the LLM (Gemma-3 for Qwen2.5-VL) and both the effect and its rough size hold up, so this looks like a general property of the pipeline family rather than a quirk of one model pairing. The upshot is that a large share of the apparent CAAP--SNAP gap traces back to closed-category annotation limits rather than a real grounding failure, which matters for how we detect hallucination, analyze failure modes, and design evaluation for grounded multimodal systems meant to work in the open world.

oai:arXiv.org:2609.32567v2.label: Attribution Gaps in Zero-Training LLM+OVOD Pipelines: A Fine-Grained Analysis of the CAAP--SNAP Discrepancy

data.title: SearchJev: A Calibrated System-1 Model for Search Agents
data.author: Congfeng Cao, Lipeng Zuo, Konstantinos Papakostas, Qiwei Xu, Songwei Xu, Qianru Meng, Lun Zhou, Zhaochun Ren, Yougang Lyu, Xiaohui Yan
data.summary: Search agents repeatedly make short decisions about relevance, evidence sufficiency, and search actions. Using generative language models for these decisions introduces latency and unreliable confidence. We present SearchJev, a calibrated System-1 model that separates search decisions from System-2 reasoning and generation. Given a search state and a decision schema, SearchJev scores legal options without autoregressive output generation. We propose Soft-Label Learning for Calibrated Decisions (SLCD) to learn decision probabilities from uncertain supervision and improve the reliability of decision confidence. In a dual-system search agent, SearchJev handles short decisions and delegates uncertain judgments to System 2, which retains planning, query generation, and answer composition. We also introduce SearchDecision-Bench, a benchmark unifying six types of search decisions for training and evaluation. On SearchDecision-Bench, SearchJev improves decision quality over same-size Qwen3.5 autoregressive models, achieves 5.2-5.3 times faster decisions, and reduces average expected calibration error by 41-74%. On BrowseComp-Plus, the dual-system agents achieve a 3.7-4.7 times speedup in active search time while improving answer accuracy from 45% to up to 54%.

data.title: SkillScreen: High-Recall Screening of Malicious Agent Skills with Decision Models
data.author: Jerrold Huang, Junwei Quan, Saiyue Lyu, Zihan Guo, Yingqiang Ge
data.summary: Agent skills turn natural-language instructions into actions, creating a security challenge: legitimate automation and malicious behaviour can look deceptively similar. A practical screen must catch nearly every attack while keeping the review load manageable. We present SkillScreen, a compact decision model trained to score skill maliciousness directly from SKILL$.$md in a single forward pass. On MaliciousSkillBench, SkillScreen flags 20-25% of benign skills at 99% recall on unseen attack families, substantially fewer than the word-level classifier and prompted LLM judges tested. Under the same training protocol, it also generalizes better than a fully fine-tuned encoder to unseen sources. Yet unfamiliar benign sources sharply increase false positives, showing that recognizing new attacks does not ensure reliable screening of new skill collections. Our results demonstrate the value of task-trained decision models for high-recall skill screening. Project page: https://jerroldh.github.io/SkillScreen-webpage/

data.title: Forecasting Brand Mentions in LLM Answers: Frozen Predictions Evaluated from Hours to Weeks
data.author: Dmitrij \.Zatuchin
data.summary: Companies and agencies now monitor which brands large language models (LLMs) name when buyers ask for recommendations. Answers vary between runs, so a single check can mislead and repeated checks cost money. We extend an earlier 20-day replication to ask how well past brand mentions predict later ones over seven weeks. We froze probabilistic forecasts before each of four prospective collection waves of Gemini 3.1 Pro answers to the same 54 buyer questions: nine question families in English, Estonian and Finnish, each for two markets, with four of 12 tracked brands per question. The waves were collected between 1.5 hours and 52 days after the history used by the earliest forecast, and each scored 648 brand and answer labels from 162 answers. A smoothed per-question history achieved a Brier score of 0.0599 at 1.5 hours, against 0.1131 for a per-brand rate and 0.25 for a constant 0.5. A pooled rate clipped to 0.05--0.95, named as the challenger before its first test, scored 0.0259 after 8 hours, 0.0269 after 30 days and 0.0328 after 52 days. Of the brand and question cells named in all or none of the earlier answers, 94.5% to 97.5% kept that pattern in each later wave, and none switched from always to never or back. With a search instruction, 100 of 162 answers returned search activity, compared with 1 of 540 earlier Pro answers; mentions stayed predictable (Brier 0.0563), and Pro history predicted a smaller model's answers less well (0.0787). Human coding agreed with 298/300 sampled automatic labels; two coders agreed on 99/100 shared items (kappa = 0.98). The results cover one provider family, a fixed candidate set and lexical mentions. They support per-question history as the baseline that any forecasting or monitoring method for LLM brand mentions should beat.

data.title: Infrathon: Benchmarking Language Agents for Real-World, Long-Horizon AI Infra Optimization
data.author: Zhengyu Hu, Zheyuan Xiao, Yike Wang, Hamish Ivison, Haoyu Wang, Yige Yuan, Rulin Shao, Yuetai Li, Niqi Lyu, Yicheng Ding, Shu Yang, Zhichen Zeng, Banghua Zhu, Jiaxin Pei, Kaize Ding, Pradeep Dasigi, Dan Roth, Hannaneh Hajishirzi, Noah A. Smith, Teng Xiao, Radha Poovendran
data.summary: In this work, we study whether frontier agents can continually improve real-world AI infrastructure over long horizons. We introduce Infrathon, a benchmark of diverse, long-horizon AI infrastructure optimization tasks across different levels. We evaluate six models across 150 runs with 24-hour budgets, totaling over 10,000 GPU-hours. Our results show that model rankings vary with the evaluation horizon, while 135 of the 150 runs achieve further improvements during the second half of their budgets. These findings indicate that shorter evaluations can overlook both optimization gains and changes in relative model performance. We also find agents can discover solutions that outperform human-designed baselines: Claude Opus 5.5 increases the mean KV-cache compression ratio from $6.82\times$ with the human-designed Quant-VideoGen codec to $19.86\times$. Analysis of agent trajectories identifies task violations, unreliable testing, and premature completion as barriers to sustained improvement. Together, our Infrathon framework provides resources for constructing long-horizon tasks, evaluating frontier agents, and discovering good infrastructure solutions. Code is available at https://github.com/InfrathonX/Infrathon
